opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting distinction, and I think it gets at something fundamental about what a world model is versus what a game engine or a simulator is.

When you control an agent, you're essentially acting *within* the world. You press forward, you turn, you jump, and the model has to figure out how the world responds to that one entity's actions. That's the classic setup, and it's what a lot of people think about when they hear "interactive world model." The agent is your point of contact with the environment.

Promptable world events are a different axis of control. Instead of acting through an agent, you're changing the world itself. You can say something like "it starts raining," or "a door opens," or "another character walks into the scene," and the model has to incorporate that into the ongoing simulation in a way that stays consistent with everything that came before. So you're less like a player and more like a director, or someone sitting at the controls of the environment.

What's exciting is that both kinds of control come out of the same underlying capability. The model is predicting how the world evolves frame by frame, conditioned on whatever signals you give it. Whether that signal is an action from the agent or a text description of an event, it's ultimately just conditioning on the dynamics. That's really different from a traditional engine, where every event has to be explicitly programmed ahead of time.

It also matters for use cases beyond entertainment. If you're thinking about training embodied agents, you want them to face situations they haven't seen, including surprising ones. Being able to inject events, like an obstacle appearing or the weather changing, lets you generate counterfactuals and edge cases on demand. So the agent is learning to act, and the world can be prompted to challenge it.

The hard part, honestly, is consistency. When you introduce an event, it has to feel like it belongs, and the world shouldn't forget what was there before. Keeping that coherence over longer horizons while still being responsive to these interventions is one of the core challenges we think about.

r001.rationale: It says promptable events change the world itself rather than acting through an agent, and gives examples such as rain or a door opening.

r002.rationale: It mentions directional actions like moving forward and turning, but does not distinguish them from commands to walk to a specified destination.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's useful to separate two very different levers you have when you're interacting with Genie. The first one is the agent's actions. That's the low-level control signal, the thing that looks like a game controller: move forward, turn left, jump. Those are local. They affect the entity you're embodying, and the world responds to them the way a physical world would.

Promptable world events are a different lever entirely. Instead of saying "I want the agent to do X," you're saying "I want the world to change." You type something like "a flock of birds flies over" or "it starts raining" or "a door opens on the left," and the model has to incorporate that into the ongoing simulation in a way that's consistent with everything it has already generated. So it's less like steering and more like being the director of the scene, or maybe the dungeon master, while the agent is still the player.

The reason I find that distinction important is that a lot of the interesting things you want to do with a world model aren't really about the agent at all. If you're training a robot policy, or an embodied agent, what you care about is coverage of situations. You want to see how it behaves when something unexpected happens, when an object appears that wasn't in the training distribution, when the lighting changes. Actions alone can't get you there, because the agent can only walk into situations that already exist in the world. World events let you inject the situations. You're essentially controlling the curriculum, not the character.

And the technical challenge that makes this hard, and honestly makes it fun, is consistency. When you prompt an event, the model can't just paste something in. It has to reconcile the event with the geometry, with the memory of what's behind you, with the agent's current state. If I say "a car drives past," it has to come from somewhere plausible and go somewhere plausible, and if I turn around three seconds later, the world should still reflect that it happened. That's the same spatial memory problem we've been pushing on for the whole project, just stressed in a new way, because now the perturbation comes from outside the agent's own causal footprint.

So the way I'd summarize it: actions control the agent, world events control everything else, and the real power is in combining them. You get an interactive environment where both the player and the designer are live, and the model is the thing that has to keep the story coherent between them.

r001.rationale: It says world events change the world independently of commands like “I want the agent to do X,” and summarizes that actions control the agent while world events control everything else.

r002.rationale: It gives directional actions such as moving forward and turning left, but does not distinguish those from destination-directed commands such as walking to a specified location.

astra-6.text:
I think of those as two complementary kinds of control. When you control an agent, you’re acting within the world—you move, you interact with things, and the world responds. With promptable world events, you can also influence what happens around that agent. You might introduce an obstacle or change the conditions, and then let the agent respond to that new situation.

That’s interesting because the agent doesn’t have to be responsible for everything that happens. You can give it a task and independently create situations that challenge it. The important thing is that those changes become part of a coherent world, so the agent can continue interacting with their consequences.

r001.rationale: It says promptable events let you independently influence what happens around the agent by introducing obstacles or changing conditions.

r002.rationale: It mentions moving and interacting, but does not distinguish commands to reach a specified destination from directional movement commands.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of those as two complementary ways of interacting with the world. When you control an agent, you’re acting through that agent—you move, you turn, you interact with what’s around you. With promptable world events, you can change something in the environment itself. You could introduce an obstacle or change the weather, and then see how the agent responds.

So you have both control over the agent’s actions and a way to influence the situations it encounters. That’s an interesting combination, because it lets you explore how an agent behaves when the world changes around it.

r001.rationale: It describes promptable world events as changing the environment itself, separately from acting through the agent.

r002.rationale: It mentions moving and turning, but does not distinguish walking to a specified destination from directional commands such as up, down, left, and right.
